title: Fermentation enhances the dietary fibre and uronic acid contents of plant foods
content:
Abstract

BACKGROUND

Epidemiological findings have repeatedly shown a positive association between dietary fibre (DF) intake and a reduced risk of non-communicable diseases. This association is primarily attributed to the ability of DF to shape the composition and metabolic activity of the gut microbiota. Plant-based foods (grains and vegetables) are rich sources of fibre, which occurs as structural polysaccharides within plant cell walls. In addition to DF, the uronic acid present as structural polysaccharides exhibits antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. This study aimed to increase the DF and uronic acid contents of grains and vegetables through natural fermentation. Twenty commonly consumed grains and vegetables were naturally fermented for 5 days, and their total, insoluble and soluble DF, non-starch polysaccharide (NSP), and uronic acid contents were measured.

RESULTS

Over the 5-day fermentation period, total, insoluble, and soluble DF, NSP and uronic acid contents increased in all samples. Notably, soluble fibre increased by 15% in kale and 60% in corn. In the remaining grains and vegetables, total DF increased by 9–111%, whereas uronic acid content increased by 23–212%. Fourier-transform infrared spectra revealed fermentation-induced structural changes in the fingerprint regions of the samples, which are consistent with polysaccharide and protein degradation and reorganisation of the plant matrix during fermentation.

CONCLUSION

These findings suggest that fermentation can be used as a strategy to enrich the DF content of grains and vegetables, potentially helping populations achieve recommended DF intake levels despite low fruit and vegetable consumption. © 2026 The Author(s).
